fact_text: Non-EEA nationals coming to work in Ireland for more than 90 days must have a contract of employment and must apply for the relevant work permission from the Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, DETE, or DFA before arriving. EU/EEA nationals (including Spanish nationals) are explicitly excluded from this requirement and do not need a work permit or employment permit to work in Ireland.

applies_to.curation_justification: fact_text: obligation on non-EEA nationals; EU/EEA explicitly excluded → non-EEA
applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can travel to Ireland on a job offer and sort the permission out after you land. Actually a non-EEA national must hold the employment contract and have applied for the work permission BEFORE arriving. Action required: start the permit application while still in Spain — arriving first does not preserve it.

evidence_quote: Before coming to work in Ireland for more than 90 days, you must have a contract of employment and you must apply for the relevant work permission to the Department of Justice to Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE) or the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA).

fact_text: The IRP (Irish Residence Permit) registration process managed by Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) applies only to nationals from countries outside the EU, UK, or Switzerland who come to Ireland to work, study, live, or join family for more than 90 days. Spanish nationals as EU citizens are not required to register with ISD under this scheme.

applies_to.curation_justification: fact_text: applies only to nationals outside EU/UK/Switzerland → non-EEA

evidence_quote: If you are from a country outside the European Union, UK or Switzerland, and come to Ireland to work, study, live or join family for more than 90 days, you must register with Immigration Service Delivery.

fact_text: Once a non-EEA national successfully registers their immigration permission, they receive an Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card by post. This card is the legal proof that the person is entitled to be in the State. For Spanish and other EU nationals, this card is not issued as they are not required to register.

applies_to.curation_justification: fact_text: card issued to registering non-EEA nationals; EU nationals not issued → non-EEA

evidence_quote: When you have successfully registered you will receive an Irish Residence Permit card by post and that is your proof that you are legally in the State.

fact_text: Once ISD grants a permission to stay in Ireland (for non-EEA nationals who need it), the person must register that permission with Irish immigration authorities within 90 days. If an appointment cannot be secured within this period, the permission will not be cancelled while waiting.
entity_title: IRP / ISD Immigration Registration (non-EEA nationals)

applies_to.curation_justification: fact_text: 90-day registration duty for non-EEA nationals who need permission → non-EEA
applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed that if you cannot get an ISD appointment inside the 90 days your permission lapses. applies_to.timing: within 90 days of ISD granting permission

evidence_quote: Once Immigration Service Delivery (ISD) grants you a permission to stay in Ireland you must register it with the Irish immigration authorities within 90 days. If you cannot get an appointment within this period don't worry – we will not cancel your permission or expect you to leave the country while you are waiting to register.

fact_text: A PPS number is mandatory when starting work in Ireland — it is needed to register with the Revenue Commissioners. Employers should not ask for a PPS number during recruitment; it is only required when the person actually takes up employment.

Action required: apply as soon as you have an address, not once you have started work.

fact_text: When applying for a PPS number, an applicant must provide proof of address using a document that shows both name and address and is not older than 3 months. Acceptable documents include: a household utility bill, an official letter or document, a bank statement, or a property lease or tenancy agreement. Third-party confirmation (e.g., from a hotel, hostel, school principal, or accommodation owner) is also accepted.

Action required: use one of the accepted alternatives — a signed lease, or third-party confirmation from a landlord, hotel, hostel or school principal — to break the circle.

Single person: €44,000 [for 2026 and 2025]

fact_text: From 1 October 2025, unearned income from rents, investments, dividends, and interest on deposits and savings is liable to PRSI at 4.2%. Anyone with unearned income over €5,000 is a chargeable person liable to pay this PRSI charge under Revenue's self-assessment system. People aged under 16 or over 70 are exempt.

fact_text: If a Spanish employer sends an employee to work in Ireland for a short assignment, the worker may continue paying social insurance in Spain under EU Regulations for up to 24 months. To benefit from this, an A1 Certificate (formerly E101 Form) must be obtained from the sending country and applied for at least 4 weeks before work begins in Ireland.
entity_title: A1 Certificate — Posted Workers from Spain (EU/EEA nationals)

applies_to.curation_justification: EU social-security coordination instrument as published (Reg 883/2004 framing). Whether it extends to third-country nationals for IRELAND (Reg 1231/2010 opt-outs) is a legal determination — NOT asserted here; see README open questions
applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the A1 can be arranged once the assignment is under way. Actually it must be applied for at least 4 weeks BEFORE work begins in Ireland; without it Irish social insurance applies instead of Spanish, and the two are not interchangeable. Action required: have the sending employer start the A1 a month before the first Irish working day.
applies_to.timing: apply at least 4 weeks before work begins in Ireland

evidence_quote: If you are employed in Ireland and your employer sends you to work temporarily in another EU state, you will continue to pay PRSI under the Irish system for 24 months. you need an A1 Certificate (formerly E101 Form) to show where you will pay your social insurance. Your employer (or you, if you are self-employed) should apply for an A1 Certificate at least 4 weeks before you start work in another EU country.

fact_text: The Universal Social Charge (USC) applies to all persons whose gross income exceeds €13,000 per year. Once income crosses this threshold, USC is charged on the full income (not just the excess). Social welfare payments and similar payments are exempt.
entity_title: Universal Social Charge — Threshold (EU/EEA nationals)

applies_to.curation_justification: USC applies to all persons over the income threshold → universal, two records
applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the €13,000 USC threshold works like a tax-free allowance, so only income above it is charged. Actually once gross income crosses €13,000 the USC is charged on the FULL amount, not just the excess. Action required: expect the whole of your income to attract USC as soon as you pass the threshold.

evidence_quote: You pay the USC if your gross income is more than €13,000 per year. Once your income is over this limit, you pay the relevant rate of USC on all of your income. If your total income is €13,000 or less per year, you do not pay any USC. If it is more than €13,000 per year, you pay USC on your full income.

fact_text: To be entitled to public health services in Ireland, a person must be ordinarily resident — meaning they have been living in Ireland for at least one year, or intend to live there for at least one year. The HSE may request proof including utility bills, bank statements, rental agreements, or official government documents not older than 12 months.
entity_title: Public Health Entitlement — Ordinary Residence (EU/EEA nationals)

applies_to.curation_justification: ordinarily-resident test governs every person's HSE entitlement → universal, two records
applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed that working and paying PRSI in Ireland entitles you to public health services straight away. Actually entitlement depends on being 'ordinarily resident' — a year's residence, or provable intent to stay a year — and the HSE can ask for utility bills, bank statements or a lease as proof. Action required: keep arrival-dated documents from day one; you may need them to prove intent.
applies_to.timing: requires one year's residence, or documented intent to stay at least one year

evidence_quote: You are ordinarily resident if you have been living in Ireland for at least a year or you intend to live here for at least one year. To check that you are ordinarily resident the HSE may ask for: Proof of property purchase or rental / A letter or statement from a financial institution / A current utility bill / A current car or home insurance policy in your name / An official document from a government department The above documents must be dated within the last 12 months.

Medical card holders are entitled to free GP services, prescribed drugs, public hospital services, dental/optical/aural services, maternity and infant care, and community care services.
